etymology: From palmer, the old name for a wandering pilgrim who journeyed with a palm branch, and worm; hence the roving caterpillar that ranges over the land devouring the green thing. In the KJV it renders the Hebrew gazam, from a root meaning “to cut off, to shear away.”
biblical_def: A palmerworm is a devouring worm or caterpillar, so called because it wanders over the land like a palmer — the old name for a pilgrim. The KJV uses it for the Hebrew gazam, from a root meaning to cut off or shear away, and it stands first in Joel’s dreadful roll-call of judgment: “That which the palmerworm hath left hath the locust eaten; and that which the locust hath left hath the cankerworm eaten; and that which the cankerworm hath left hath the caterpiller eaten” (Joe 1:4). Four devourers in rank, each finishing what the last began, until nothing green remains. Amos names the same creature among the LORD’s chastenings: blasting and mildew came, and then “the palmerworm devoured them: yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD” (Amo 4:9). Here is the doctrine. The palmerworm is no accident of nature but a servant of God, sent to strip a people that would not repent; and the sorrow of it is not the wasted vine but the unturned heart. Yet the same prophet who counted the devourers heard the promise: “I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten” (Joe 2:25) — and the LORD there calls them my great army, His own hosts under His own command. The God who sends the palmerworm is the God who restores the years it ate, and He bids the stripped nation rend the heart and turn to Him, “for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness” (Joe 2:13).
webster_summary: A devouring worm or caterpillar that wanders over the land and strips the green thing; in the KJV the Hebrew gazam, first of Joel’s four devourers.

corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but an old name for a devouring worm; it recovers that God commands the devourer and restores the years it ate.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes an age that reads calamity without a Sender. Amos rehearses blasting, mildew, and the palmerworm, and the refrain after each stroke is the same: “yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD.” The chastening was not chiefly the loss of the crop but the appeal of a God who struck to draw His people home, and the sin was not the eating of the vine but the unturned heart. Men who see only weather in a wasted field will miss the voice in it, and the palmerworm will have come for nothing. God does not strip a people to ruin them but to bring them back.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the devourer is God’s own. The LORD calls the palmerworm and its fellows “my great army which I sent among you” — they march at His word and halt at His word, and not a leaf is eaten but by His command. That is why the promise can stand: “I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten.” A God who merely permitted the ruin could not promise the restoring; the God who sent the army can give back the years. Let the stripped soul rend the heart and not the garments and turn unto the LORD, for He is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness.

etymology: From canker (through Old French from the Latin cancer, “a crab, an eating sore”) and worm; hence the worm that eats as a canker eats, spreading and hollowing what it feeds upon. In the KJV it renders the Hebrew yeleq, the licking or gnawing locust.
biblical_def: The cankerworm is the worm that eats as a canker eats — slowly, spreadingly, until the thing consumed is hollow. It renders the Hebrew yeleq, a word for the licking or gnawing locust, and it takes its place in Joel’s rank of judgment: “that which the locust hath left hath the cankerworm eaten; and that which the cankerworm hath left hath the caterpiller eaten” (Joe 1:4). It is the middle of the ruin, neither the first bite nor the last, and it leaves less than it found. Nahum takes the same creature and turns it upon Nineveh, that great and merchant city: “There shall the fire devour thee; the sword shall cut thee off, it shall eat thee up like the cankerworm: make thyself many as the cankerworm, make thyself many as the locusts” (Nah 3:15). Let the city breed and multiply as the swarm does — it shall be eaten as the swarm eats. And the sting is in the next verse: “Thou hast multiplied thy merchants above the stars of heaven: the cankerworm spoileth, and flieth away” (Nah 3:16). There is the picture of every merchant glory. The cankerworm gorges, then spreads its wings and is gone, leaving the branch bare; so Nineveh’s traders swarmed while the gain lasted and vanished when the judgment came. Yet over the whole ruin stands the promise: “I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you” (Joe 2:25).
webster_summary: A worm that preys upon leaf and fruit, eating as a canker eats; in the KJV the Hebrew yeleq, the licking locust.
webster_full: CANKERWORM, a worm that preys upon fruit and leaves, eating as a canker eats.
From canker, Latin cancer, “a crab, a spreading sore,” and worm.
In the KJV it renders the Hebrew yeleq, the licking or gnawing locust.
It is the third of the four devourers in Joel’s judgment (Joe 1:4).
It figures the merchants of Nineveh, who spoil and fly away (Nah 3:16).
scriptures: Joe 1:4
That which the palmerworm hath left hath the locust eaten; and that which the locust hath left hath the cankerworm eaten; and that which the cankerworm hath left hath the caterpiller eaten.
Nah 3:15
There shall the fire devour thee; the sword shall cut thee off, it shall eat thee up like the cankerworm: make thyself many as the cankerworm, make thyself many as the locusts.
Nah 3:16
Thou hast multiplied thy merchants above the stars of heaven: the cankerworm spoileth, and flieth away.
Joe 2:25
And I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but an old name for a gnawing worm; it recovers that merchant glory spoils and flies away, and that God restores what the devourer ate.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a live misuse of the world’s goods here, and Nahum names it. Nineveh multiplied her merchants above the stars of heaven and thought herself established for ever; but the cankerworm spoileth, and flieth away. That is the whole history of commerce without God — the swarm settles where the gain is, strips the branch, and takes wing at the first cold, and the city that trusted the swarm is left with bare wood. An age that measures a nation by its traffic and reckons the merchant the surest man alive is reading the branch and not the worm. Riches make themselves wings and fly away as an eagle toward heaven.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the restoring hand of God. The cankerworm eats what the locust left and leaves less than it found, and no man can put back a devoured year. But the LORD says, “I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm, my great army which I sent among you.” The devourers were His to send and the years are His to give back. What sin has eaten out of a life, grace can restore — not by undoing the ruin but by a mercy that outweighs it, in Christ, who was Himself consumed that His people might be made whole.

etymology: The KJV’s spelling of caterpillar, from the Old French chatepelose, “hairy cat,” from the shagginess of the creature; hence the devouring larva. In Joel it renders the Hebrew chasil, from a root meaning “to consume, to finish off.”
biblical_def: Caterpiller is the KJV’s spelling of caterpillar, and in Joel it is the last of the four devourers, rendering the Hebrew chasil, from a root meaning to consume or to finish off. It comes at the end of the roll: “that which the cankerworm hath left hath the caterpiller eaten” (Joe 1:4) — the finisher, that takes the last leaf the others spared. In the psalm of Israel’s history the caterpiller is one of the plagues upon Egypt: “He gave also their increase unto the caterpiller, and their labour unto the locust” (Psa 78:46). Mark the word gave. Egypt’s increase did not fall to the worm by chance; God gave it. The whole labour of a mighty nation was handed over to a crawling thing, that Pharaoh might learn who reigns. Isaiah uses the creature for the plunder of Assyria’s host: “your spoil shall be gathered like the gathering of the caterpiller: as the running to and fro of locusts shall he run upon them” (Isa 33:4) — the spoiler is spoiled, and the plunder is stripped from him as swiftly as a swarm strips a field. So the caterpiller is God’s finishing servant, sent upon Egypt, upon Assyria, and upon a backslidden Israel alike. And to the last of the devourers the last of the promises is joined: “I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, the cankerworm, and the caterpiller, and the palmerworm” (Joe 2:25). What God gave to the worm, God can give back.
webster_summary: The KJV’s spelling of caterpillar; the devouring larva that finishes what the other worms leave, rendering the Hebrew chasil.
webster_full: CATERPILLER, the KJV spelling of caterpillar; the worm-like larva that devours leaves and herbage.

God gave Egypt’s increase unto the caterpiller (Psa 78:46).

corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but an old spelling for a devouring larva; it recovers that God gives the harvest to the worm and takes back what He gave.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the notion of a world that runs itself. “He gave also their increase unto the caterpiller” — the psalmist will not say that Egypt suffered a blight; he says God gave the increase away. The labour of a mighty kingdom was handed over to a crawling worm by the deliberate act of the LORD, and the plague was a sermon to Pharaoh on who governs the field. To read such a judgment as bad seasons and poor husbandry is to be blinder than Pharaoh, who at least knew that he was being struck and by whom.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereignty of God over the smallest creature and the largest empire. He set the caterpiller upon Egypt’s increase, and He ordered the spoiler’s spoil to be gathered like the gathering of the caterpiller, stripping Assyria as swiftly as a swarm strips a field. The same hand that gives to the worm restores the years the worm ate. Nothing is too small to be His servant and nothing too great to be His subject; and the God who commands the caterpiller commands the whole account of a man’s losses, and can give them back.

etymology: From the Latin unicornis, “one-horned,” from unus (“one”) and cornu (“horn”), through Old French; the Authorized Version’s rendering of the Hebrew re’em, a great wild ox of the waste places, following the Septuagint’s monokeros.
biblical_def: The unicorn of the Authorized Version is not the horse of fable but the Hebrew re’em, a great wild ox of prodigious strength — a real beast, roaming the waste places, that no man could yoke to a plough. The AV translators followed the Septuagint’s monokeros and the Latin unicornis, “one-horned,” and gave the creature the English name then to hand. What Scripture says of it is not fabulous at all but plain: it is untamable, it is mighty, and its horns are terrible. Balaam, compelled to bless where he came to curse, says: “God brought them out of Egypt; he hath as it were the strength of an unicorn” (Num 23:22). That is the whole doctrine of the Exodus in a figure — Israel had no strength of her own, but the LORD who redeemed her was strong as the wild ox, and Balak’s enchantments could no more turn Him than a man could rein the re’em. Moses blesses Joseph with the same image: “his horns are like the horns of unicorns: with them he shall push the people together to the ends of the earth” (Deu 33:17). David prays out of the depth, “save me from the lion’s mouth: for thou hast heard me from the horns of the unicorns” (Psa 22:21), and in another psalm rejoices, “my horn shalt thou exalt like the horn of an unicorn” (Psa 92:10). The horn is strength; the unicorn is strength unbroken; and every time the figure is used, the strength turns out to be God’s.
webster_summary: A one-horned beast; in the KJV the Hebrew re’em, a great wild ox of untamable strength whose horns are the figure of power.
webster_full: UNICORN, literally a one-horned animal; from the Latin unus, “one,” and cornu, “horn.”
In the KJV it renders the Hebrew re’em, a great wild ox of the waste places.

Scripture names the beast untamable, mighty, and terrible in its horns (Job 39:9-10).
Its strength figures the power of God, who brought Israel out of Egypt (Num 23:22).
scriptures: God brought them out of Egypt; he hath as it were the strength of an unicorn.

His glory is like the firstling of his bullock, and his horns are like the horns of unicorns: with them he shall push the people together to the ends of the earth: and they are the ten thousands of Ephraim, and they are the thousands of Manasseh.
Save me from the lion's mouth: for thou hast heard me from the horns of the unicorns.
But my horn shalt thou exalt like the horn of an unicorn: I shall be anointed with fresh oil.
corruption_summary: Skeptics point at the AV’s “unicorn” to mock Scripture as fable; but the Hebrew re’em is a real beast of real strength, and the mockery trades a question about English for a charge against inspiration.
corruption_paragraphs: Here is a live corruption, and it must be answered straight. The scoffer opens the Authorized Version, finds the word unicorn, and declares that the Bible teaches fairy tales — and from that he means to argue that Scripture is not to be trusted at all. The charge is a sleight of hand. The Hebrew word is re’em, and what the text says of the creature is the opposite of fable: it is a beast of enormous strength that cannot be bound with his band in the furrow nor trusted to bring home the seed (Job 39:9-10), whose horns push the nations to the ends of the earth. That is a description of a living animal in the waste places, and the mocker never engages it. The AV translators, following the Septuagint’s monokeros and the Latin unicornis, rendered a great one-horned wild ox with the English word then available for a one-horned beast. Whether a later English word would serve the modern reader better is a question about English; it is not a question about inspiration. The scoffer swaps the one for the other and hopes no one notices.

So the line must be drawn on both sides, and drawn honestly. We concede nothing on inerrancy: the Word of God given in the Hebrew and the Greek is without error, and no man has yet shown an error in the re’em. Neither do we pretend that the KJV’s English is beyond all revision — it is a translation, made by men, out of a providentially preserved text, and its renderings are as revisable as the English tongue itself. To confound the two is the very confusion the mocker trades upon: a question of vocabulary is dressed up as a verdict against the Holy Ghost. What Scripture affirms is the strength, and the strength stands. The LORD brought Israel out of Egypt with the strength of an unicorn, and neither the enchantments of Balaam nor the wit of the scoffer can turn Him. It is better to fear that strength than to laugh at the word chosen for it.

My horn shalt thou exalt like the horn of an unicorn: the saint’s strength is a gift, not a possession.
The re’em cannot be bound in the furrow; the mocker’s fable is not the Bible’s beast.

etymology: From the Latin ossifraga, “the bone-breaker,” from os (“a bone”) and frangere (“to break”); so named from the bird’s manner of bearing bones aloft and letting them fall upon the rocks to shatter them for the marrow.
biblical_def: The ossifrage is the bone-breaker — a great bird of prey named in the Latin ossifraga, from its manner of bearing bones aloft and dropping them upon the rocks to shatter them for the marrow. It appears twice in all Scripture, and both times in the same list: among the fowls that Israel might not eat. “These are they which ye shall have in abomination among the fowls… the eagle, and the ossifrage, and the ospray” (Lev 11:13); and again in Moses’ rehearsal of the law, “these are they of which ye shall not eat: the eagle, and the ossifrage, and the ospray” (Deu 14:12). The bird heads the roll of the unclean fowls with the eagle and the ospray — the birds of talon and carrion, that feed upon blood and bone. The purpose of the law is stated plainly: it was given “to make a difference between the unclean and the clean, and between the beast that may be eaten and the beast that may not be eaten” (Lev 11:47). Israel’s table was a daily catechism in separation: a holy people, set apart to a holy God, learned holiness by what they would not touch. The ossifrage was no more sinful than the sparrow — it was a sign. And when the sign had done its work the Lord took it away, letting down the sheet from heaven and answering “I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean” (Act 10:14) with a word that cleansed the meat and opened the door to the Gentiles.
webster_summary: The bone-breaker; a great bird of prey that drops bones upon the rocks to break them, named among the unclean fowls of the law.
webster_full: OSSIFRAGE, the bone-breaker; a large bird of prey of the eagle kind.
From the Latin os, “a bone,” and frangere, “to break.”
So named from bearing bones aloft and dropping them on the rocks for the marrow.
It stands with the eagle and the ospray among the unclean fowls (Lev 11:13).
It occurs but twice in Scripture, both times in the roll of forbidden birds (Deu 14:12).
scriptures: And these are they which ye shall have in abomination among the fowls; they shall not be eaten, they are an abomination: the eagle, and the ossifrage, and the ospray,
But these are they of which ye shall not eat: the eagle, and the ossifrage, and the ospray,
To make a difference between the unclean and the clean, and between the beast that may be eaten and the beast that may not be eaten.
But Peter said, Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but an old name for a bird of prey; it recovers that the law of clean and unclean taught separation, and that Christ has cleansed the meat.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes two errors at once, and they lean opposite ways. The first would keep the shadow: to hold the ossifrage and the ospray still forbidden is to bind the conscience where Christ has loosed it, for the Lord let down the sheet from heaven and said, what God hath cleansed, that call not thou common. The second would despise the shadow: to read Leviticus as arbitrary taboo, a relic of a superstitious people, is to miss that Israel’s table was a daily catechism, teaching a nation to make a difference between the clean and the unclean, and so to learn that their God is holy and they must be a separated people.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the ceremonial sign is fulfilled, not forgotten. The dietary law was never about the digestion; it was about the difference. The bone-breaker was no more sinful than the sparrow, but it was set on the wrong side of a line God drew to teach His people what separation means. In Christ the line is not erased but moved inward: the meat is clean and the Gentile is welcome, and what remains is the very substance the sign was shadowing — be ye holy, for I am holy. The Christian’s separation is no longer from the ossifrage but from the world, the flesh, and the devil.

etymology: From the Old English hwelp, “the young of a dog or of any beast of prey”; hence a cub, chiefly the young of the lion.
biblical_def: A whelp is the young of a beast of prey — the cub, chiefly of the lion. Scripture’s greatest use of the word is Jacob’s dying blessing upon his fourth son: “Judah is a lion’s whelp: from the prey, my son, thou art gone up: he stooped down, he couched as a lion, and as an old lion; who shall rouse him up?” (Gen 49:9). The blessing goes on to say that the sceptre shall not depart from Judah until Shiloh come; so the whelp is a prophecy. Out of the tribe of Judah would come the King, and the young lion of the blessing grows into the crouching lion whom none dares rouse. The Revelation names Him: “behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book” (Rev 5:5). Judah’s whelp is Jesus Christ, and He who was slain as a Lamb has prevailed as a Lion. Elsewhere the word marks the pride of the wicked and its end. Nahum taunts Nineveh, that den of lions: “where is the dwelling of the lions… where the lion, even the old lion, walked, and the lion’s whelp, and none made them afraid?” (Nah 2:11). The whelps of Assyria fed on torn nations and were themselves torn. Job speaks the same law: “the old lion perisheth for lack of prey, and the stout lion’s whelps are scattered abroad” (Job 4:11). Every lion of the earth is scattered at the last; only the Lion of Judah reigns.
webster_summary: The young of a beast of prey, chiefly of the lion; in Genesis the figure of Judah, out of whose tribe the Lion should come.
webster_full: WHELP, the young of a dog, a lion, or other beast of prey; a cub.
From the Old English hwelp.
Jacob blessed Judah as a lion’s whelp gone up from the prey (Gen 49:9).
It marks the lions of Nineveh, whose den was made desolate (Nah 2:11).
The stout lion’s whelps are scattered abroad at the last (Job 4:11).

Nah 2:11

corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but the old word for a lion’s cub; it recovers Jacob’s prophecy of Judah and the Lion of the tribe of Juda who has prevailed.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes an age that wants a tame Christ. Jacob’s blessing does not make Judah a household pet but a lion’s whelp gone up from the prey, that stoops and couches and dares any man to rouse him. The Christ of Scripture is the Lamb slain and the Lion of the tribe of Juda, and the very hands that were pierced hold the book of judgment. A gospel that keeps the Lamb and quietly drops the Lion has kept half a Saviour, and it is not the half that opens the seals.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the long faithfulness of God to His promise. Jacob spoke over a whelp and prophesied a sceptre that would not depart from Judah until Shiloh came; and the centuries rolled, and the tribe was carried to Babylon and brought back and ground under Rome, and still the word held. Then John wept because none was found worthy to open the book, and an elder said, weep not, behold the Lion of the tribe of Juda hath prevailed. From the dying bed of a patriarch to the throne of heaven, the promise did not fail. Every lion of the earth perisheth for lack of prey and his whelps are scattered abroad; the Lion of Judah reigns for ever.
roots_summary: The word means the young of a beast of prey, chiefly the lion’s cub.

The whelp of Judah is the Lion of the tribe of Juda (Rev 5:5).
usage: Judah is a lion’s whelp: the blessing was a prophecy of the King to come.
The whelps of Nineveh fed on torn nations, and their den was made desolate.
The Lion of the tribe of Juda hath prevailed — Jacob’s whelp is Christ enthroned.

etymology: The old English plural of beef, from the Old French boef, from the Latin bos, bovis, “an ox”; hence oxen, the cattle of the herd — the living beasts, not the meat cut from them.
biblical_def: Beeves is the old English plural of beef — not the meat but the beasts: oxen, the cattle of the herd. The KJV uses it where the herd is offered or numbered, and it belongs chiefly to two places. The first is the law of offering. “Ye shall offer at your own will a male without blemish, of the beeves, of the sheep, or of the goats” (Lev 22:19); and again, “whosoever offereth a sacrifice of peace offerings unto the LORD to accomplish his vow, or a freewill offering in beeves or sheep, it shall be perfect to be accepted; there shall be no blemish therein” (Lev 22:21). Two things are fixed there: the offering is of a man’s own will, and it must be perfect. Willing and spotless — God will take neither a forced gift nor a flawed one. The second place is the spoil of Midian, where Moses numbers the herds and levies the LORD’s tribute upon them: “levy a tribute unto the LORD of the men of war which went out to battle: one soul of five hundred, both of the persons, and of the beeves, and of the asses, and of the sheep” (Num 31:28), and the tally is set down — “threescore and twelve thousand beeves” (Num 31:33). Even the plunder of a battle is counted before God. So the beeves preach worship in one homely word: what comes to us is reckoned, what we bring must be willing and perfect, and Christ alone was the offering without blemish.
webster_summary: The old plural of beef; oxen, the cattle of the herd, as offered in sacrifice and numbered in the spoil.
webster_full: BEEVES, the plural of beef; cattle, oxen of the herd.
From the Old French boef, Latin bos, bovis, “an ox.”
It names the living beasts, not the meat cut from them.
Of the beeves a male without blemish might be offered (Lev 22:19).
The beeves of the Midianite spoil were numbered and tithed to the LORD (Num 31:28).

corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but the old plural for cattle; it recovers that an offering must be willing and without blemish, and that the spoil itself is counted before God.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the grudging and the shabby in worship. The law of the beeves is exact: the offering is at a man’s own will, and it shall be perfect to be accepted; there shall be no blemish therein. God is not served by a gift wrung out of a man, nor by the beast he was glad to be rid of. Malachi’s people brought the lame and the sick and supposed the altar would not know the difference, and the LORD bade them offer it now unto their governor and see whether he would be pleased. What a man would not dare give his employer he brings to God, and calls it worship.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the beeves point past themselves. No ox of the herd, however spotless, ever took away a sin; the blood of bulls and of goats could not do it. The perfect male without blemish was a picture drawn in cattle of the Lamb without blemish and without spot, who offered Himself willingly — “lo, I come to do thy will, O God” — and was accepted for His people once for all. Willing and spotless: the law demanded both of the beeves, and found both only in Christ.
roots_summary: The word means cattle, oxen of the herd — the old plural of beef.
roots_lines: Beeves — the old English plural of beef.
From Old French boef, from Latin bos, bovis, “an ox.”
It names the living beasts of the herd, not the meat.
Of the beeves the offering must be male and without blemish (Lev 22:19).
The beeves of the spoil were numbered and the LORD’s tribute levied (Num 31:28).
usage: A male without blemish, of the beeves — God takes no flawed gift to His altar.
A freewill offering in beeves shall be perfect to be accepted: willing and spotless both.
Even the beeves of the spoil were counted, and a tribute levied unto the LORD.

etymology: From fat and the diminutive ending -ling; hence a young beast fattened for the slaughter — the choice, well-fed animal of the herd or the flock, the best a man has.
biblical_def: A fatling is a beast fattened for the slaughter — the choice animal of the herd. Rightly used it is the costliest worship: “I will offer unto thee burnt sacrifices of fatlings, with the incense of rams; I will offer bullocks with goats” (Psa 66:15). But the word’s hardest lesson is Saul’s. Commanded to destroy Amalek utterly, “Saul and the people spared Agag, and the best of the sheep, and of the oxen, and of the fatlings, and the lambs, and all that was good, and would not utterly destroy them: but every thing that was vile and refuse, that they destroyed utterly” (1Sa 15:9). Mark the shape of the disobedience. Saul destroyed the worthless and kept the valuable, and told Samuel he had spared the best to sacrifice them unto the LORD. It is the perfect picture of religion made a cloak for self-will: the fatlings would look very holy upon the altar, and they were the very thing God had said to kill. Samuel’s answer is the sentence over all such worship: “Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams” (1Sa 15:22). A kingdom was torn away that day over a herd of fat cattle. Yet the word ends in peace: in the day of the LORD’s King, “the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them” (Isa 11:6).
webster_summary: A young beast fattened for the slaughter; the choice animal of the herd, offered in sacrifice — and the thing Saul spared in disobedience.
webster_full: FATLING, a young animal fattened for slaughter; a fat beast of the herd or flock.
From fat and the diminutive ending -ling.
The fatlings were among the costliest of burnt sacrifices (Psa 66:15).
Saul spared the fatlings of Amalek and lost his kingdom (1Sa 15:9).
In the peaceable kingdom the fatling lies down with the young lion (Isa 11:6).
scriptures: But Saul and the people spared Agag, and the best of the sheep, and of the oxen, and of the fatlings, and the lambs, and all that was good, and would not utterly destroy them: but every thing that was vile and refuse, that they destroyed utterly.
And Samuel said, Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.
I will offer unto thee burnt sacrifices of fatlings, with the incense of rams; I will offer bullocks with goats. Selah.
Isa 11:6
The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but the old word for a fattened beast; it recovers that to obey is better than sacrifice, and that spared fatlings cost Saul a kingdom.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the oldest dodge in religion: obeying God in the part that costs nothing and calling the remainder an offering. Saul destroyed everything vile and refuse and spared the best of the fatlings, and had a pious reason ready — they were to be sacrificed unto the LORD. So a man will tithe the mint and the anise and leave the weightier matters of the law; he will give God the loud offering and withhold the quiet obedience. The fatling upon the altar looks like devotion and is disobedience with a religious face, and God is not deceived by the smoke of it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Samuel’s: to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams. God is not hungry, and He is not bribed. He asks for the man and not the beast, and an offering brought instead of obedience is rebellion dressed for church. Saul kept the fatlings and lost the kingdom; and the true King, when He came, said not “I bring fatlings” but “lo, I come to do thy will, O God.” Christ’s obedience is the sacrifice in which God delights, and the believer’s obedience is the fruit of it, never the price of it.
roots_summary: The word means a young beast fattened for the slaughter, the choice of the herd.
roots_lines: Fatling — from fat and the diminutive ending -ling.
It denotes a young beast fattened for the knife, the best of the herd.
Fatlings were offered as the costliest of burnt sacrifices (Psa 66:15).
Saul spared the fatlings of Amalek and was rejected from being king (1Sa 15:9).
In the peaceable kingdom the fatling lies down with the young lion (Isa 11:6).
usage: Saul spared the fatlings and destroyed the refuse — obedience only where it cost him nothing.
To obey is better than sacrifice: a fat beast on the altar cannot buy a rebel’s pardon.
The calf and the young lion and the fatling together: the knife and the tooth shall rest at last.

etymology: The KJV’s spelling of grizzled, from the Old French grisel, a diminutive of gris, “grey”; hence flecked or patched with grey, of a mottled and mixed colour.
biblical_def: Grisled is the KJV’s spelling of grizzled — flecked or patched with grey, of a mottled colour. It occurs in two places only, and both are worth the reader’s eye. The first is Jacob’s account of how the LORD made him rich in Laban’s house against Laban’s will: “I lifted up mine eyes, and saw in a dream, and, behold, the rams which leaped upon the cattle were ringstraked, speckled, and grisled” (Gen 31:10). Laban had changed his servant’s wages ten times, and every time God turned the herd to the colour Jacob was owed. The angel says so plainly: “Lift up now thine eyes, and see, all the rams which leap upon the cattle are ringstraked, speckled, and grisled: for I have seen all that Laban doeth unto thee” (Gen 31:12). The markings of cattle are in the hand of God: He sees the cheating of a master and answers it in the colour of the lambs. The second place is Zechariah’s vision of the four chariots that come from between two mountains of brass: “in the third chariot white horses; and in the fourth chariot grisled and bay horses” (Zec 6:3); and of the fourth it is said, “the grisled go forth toward the south country” (Zec 6:6). These are the spirits of the heavens, sent to walk to and fro through the earth at the word of the Lord of all the earth. Grey or white or black, they go where He sends them. The same providence that speckled Jacob’s flock drives the chariots of heaven.
webster_summary: The KJV’s spelling of grizzled; flecked or streaked with grey, of a mottled and mixed colour.
webster_full: GRISLED, the KJV spelling of grizzled; grey, or interspersed with grey; of a mixed colour.
From the Old French grisel, a diminutive of gris, “grey.”
It describes the ringstraked and speckled cattle of Jacob’s wages (Gen 31:10).
It describes the horses of Zechariah’s fourth chariot (Zec 6:3).
It occurs in these two places only in all the Scripture.
scriptures: And it came to pass at the time that the cattle conceived, that I lifted up mine eyes, and saw in a dream, and, behold, the rams which leaped upon the cattle were ringstraked, speckled, and grisled.
And he said, Lift up now thine eyes, and see, all the rams which leap upon the cattle are ringstraked, speckled, and grisled: for I have seen all that Laban doeth unto thee.
Zec 6:3
And in the third chariot white horses; and in the fourth chariot grisled and bay horses.
Zec 6:6
The black horses which are therein go forth into the north country; and the white go forth after them; and the grisled go forth toward the south country.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but an old word for grey-flecked; it recovers a providence that reaches to the colour of a lamb and to the horses of heaven.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes a small view of providence. Laban changed his servant’s wages ten times, and each time God changed the flock to match — ringstraked, speckled, grisled, whatever Jacob was owed. The angel gives the reason: “I have seen all that Laban doeth unto thee.” God is not indifferent to a cheated workman, and He does not wait upon the courts. He answers in the very currency of the fraud, and the defrauder watches his own herd turn against him. Let no man think his master’s dealings beneath heaven’s notice, and let no master think his book-keeping is hidden.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reach of that same government. The hand that mottled the lambs in Padanaram drives the four chariots out from between the mountains of brass, and the grisled horses go forth toward the south country because the Lord of all the earth has sent them. There is no realm too small for Him and none too great. The believer who trusts God with the nations may safely trust Him with his wages; and the believer who has seen Him keep the wages may safely trust Him with the nations. He that numbers the grey hairs in a lamb’s coat numbers the very hairs of your head.

roots_lines: Grisled — the KJV’s spelling of grizzled.
From Old French grisel, a diminutive of gris, “grey.”
It denotes a coat flecked or patched with grey, of a mixed colour.
It marks the cattle God gave Jacob against Laban’s fraud (Gen 31:10).
It marks the horses of Zechariah’s fourth chariot (Zec 6:3).
usage: The rams were ringstraked, speckled, and grisled — God paid Jacob out of Laban’s own herd.
I have seen all that Laban doeth unto thee: heaven keeps the books of a cheated workman.
The grisled horses go forth toward the south country at the word of the Lord of all the earth.

etymology: From the Old French veneison, from the Latin venatio, “hunting, the chase, that which is taken in hunting,” from venari, “to hunt”; hence the flesh of game — not deer-meat only, but any meat taken in the chase.
biblical_def: Venison is the flesh of the hunt — not deer-meat only, but any game taken in the chase. It belongs almost wholly to one sad household. “Isaac loved Esau, because he did eat of his venison: but Rebekah loved Jacob” (Gen 25:28). The Holy Ghost is candid about a patriarch: Isaac’s love for his elder son ran along the line of his palate, and the partiality that split the house began at the table. It is a real fault in a real man of God, set down without excuse. That appetite governs the whole of the sorry business that follows. Old and blind, Isaac sends Esau out: “take, I pray thee, thy weapons, thy quiver and thy bow, and go out to the field, and take me some venison” (Gen 27:3) — he will bless where he is fed. And Jacob, dressed in his brother’s garments, says, “arise, I pray thee, sit and eat of my venison, that thy soul may bless me” (Gen 27:19); the blessing is got by a lie because it was already being sold for a meal. Esau is the other half of the same sin. He had traded the birthright for a mess of pottage, and the Holy Ghost names him for it: “lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright” (Heb 12:16). Profane — a man who counted the holy thing worth a dinner. Venison is the taste that ruled a father and the appetite that undid a son.
webster_summary: The flesh of game taken in hunting; in Genesis, the meat Isaac loved and the appetite that ruled a house.
webster_full: VENISON, the flesh of beasts of the chase; game taken in hunting.
From the Latin venatio, “hunting,” from venari, “to hunt.”
It is not deer-flesh only, but any meat of the hunt.
Isaac loved Esau because he did eat of his venison (Gen 25:28).
The blessing was sought over a dish of venison and got by a lie (Gen 27:19).
scriptures: And Isaac loved Esau, because he did eat of his venison: but Rebekah loved Jacob.
Gen 27:3
Now therefore take, I pray thee, thy weapons, thy quiver and thy bow, and go out to the field, and take me some venison;
And Jacob said unto his father, I am Esau thy firstborn; I have done according as thou badest me: arise, I pray thee, sit and eat of my venison, that thy soul may bless me.
Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but the old word for game; it recovers Isaac’s appetite-driven partiality as a real fault, and Esau the profane person who sold the birthright for a meal.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes a religion of the appetite. Isaac loved Esau because he did eat of his venison — Scripture says it flatly and does not soften it for a patriarch. A father’s love ran along the line of his stomach; the partiality bred a rival partiality in his wife; the house was split, a dying man was deceived, and two brothers were parted for twenty years. There is no whitewash here. The Bible tells the truth about its own, and the truth about this one is that a fault as small as a taste for game grew into a household torn in two. Let the man who governs a house ask first what governs him.

The other half of the lesson is Esau’s, and it is heavier. The Holy Ghost sets him up as the warning of the whole epistle: “lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright.” Profane is the word — not wicked in some spectacular way, but common, a man to whom holy things were ordinary and a hot meal was pressing. He did not hate the birthright; he simply wanted his dinner more, and afterward he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears. That is how souls are lost: not commonly by a great crime, but by a small appetite that would not wait. Venison for a birthright is the worst bargain in Scripture, and men make it every day.
roots_summary: The word means the flesh of game taken in the hunt.
